summary: Specifies an extension to BCP 47 language tags that carries language or locale-based behavior and refinements, based on work by the Unicode Consortium. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Language labels like "English" can get extra bits saying things such as which calendar or sort order to use. This defines those extra bits.

questions: how to add locale preferences to language tags
subtitle: Extending language tags with Unicode locale data

tldr.problem: Language tags like 'en-US' identify a language and region, but applications need to specify additional locale preferences such as calendar systems, sorting order, or number formatting.
tldr.mechanism: The 'u' extension to BCP 47 adds a structured set of attributes and key-value pairs to language tags, sourced from Unicode Technical Standard 35 (LDML), allowing applications to encode locale-specific behavior alongside the base language tag.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now request specific localization options (like phonebook-style collation in German) without needing separate locale configuration, making language tags self-contained.

today: RFC 6067 is an Informational specification and has not been obsoleted or updated. The Unicode locale extension is widely used in web browsers, mobile operating systems, and server-side localization frameworks to specify locale preferences without requiring separate configuration files.

sections.title: Language Tags and Localization
sections.content:
Language tags, as defined by RFC 5646 (BCP 47), identify the language of content. They use codes like 'en' for English, 'de' for German, and can be refined with region codes like 'en-US' for American English. These tags are also used as locale identifiers in operating systems and APIs.

However, language and region alone do not specify all the details needed for proper localization. Applications need to know additional preferences such as which calendar to use (Gregorian, Islamic, Japanese), how to sort text (dictionary order or phonebook order for German), which currency to display, or whether to use a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. The Unicode Consortium maintains standardized data for these preferences in a resource called the Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR).
sections.eli5: A language tag like 'de-DE' says 'German in Germany'. But speakers might want phonebook-style sorting for names or a specific calendar. This extension lets you add those choices to the tag itself.

sections.title: The 'u' Extension
sections.content:
RFC 6067 defines the Unicode locale extension, identified by the singleton letter 'u'. When added to a language tag, it is followed by a series of subtags that specify locale preferences. For example, the tag 'de-DE-u-co-phonebk' specifies German in Germany with phonebook-style collation (co = collation, phonebk = phonebook).

The extension subtags are organized into two categories: attributes and keywords. Attributes are optional and rarely used; keywords are the primary mechanism. Each keyword consists of a two-character key (like 'co' for collation) followed by zero or more type subtags that specify the value (like 'phonebk'). The key 'ca' specifies the calendar, 'nu' specifies the number system, and 'tz' specifies the time zone.
sections.eli5: The extension works like adding labels to a package. The 'u' says 'here come locale preferences', then two-letter codes (called keys) like 'ca' or 'co' name the preference, and longer codes name the value.

sections.title: Structure of Subtags
sections.content:
All subtags in the 'u' extension follow strict formatting rules. Attributes are 3 to 8 characters long and appear before any keywords. Keys are exactly 2 characters long. Types (the values that follow a key) are 3 to 8 characters long. All are composed of ASCII letters and digits, are case-insensitive, and must not exceed 8 characters.

The extension is never case-sensitive, but the canonical form is always lowercase. When multiple keys appear in a tag, they must be in US-ASCII order. The order of type subtags within a single keyword matters to interpretation; reordering them can change meaning. For example, the 'co' (collation) key can have multiple type values that apply in sequence.
sections.eli5: The rules are strict: keys are always 2 letters, types are 3 to 8 letters, everything is lowercase in the standard form, and the order of types within a key can matter.

sections.title: Authority and Maintenance
sections.content:
The Unicode Consortium maintains and publishes the definition of valid attributes, keys, and types in Unicode Technical Standard 35 (LDML), the Unicode Locale Data Markup Language. Once defined, these subtags are never removed and never change in meaning, ensuring backward compatibility. The Consortium publishes machine-readable files listing all valid subtags, updated with each new version of LDML.

RFC 6067 itself only defines the syntax and registration mechanism; it does not enumerate the specific keys and types. Instead, it delegates that authority to the Unicode Consortium via a formal registration with IANA. The Consortium can add new keys and types in future versions of LDML without requiring a new RFC, provided the changes are backward-compatible.
sections.eli5: The Unicode group (not the IETF) decides what locale preferences exist and publishes a list. Once something is on the list, it never disappears or changes meaning.

sections.title: Normalization and Interoperability
sections.content:
To ensure that different systems interpret the same tag consistently, RFC 6067 defines a canonical form. The canonical form uses lowercase letters for all subtags, and places attributes and keywords in a specific order: attributes in US-ASCII order (numbers before letters), then keywords sorted by their 2-character key in US-ASCII order. The type subtags within each keyword retain their original order, since reordering them would change the meaning.

Applications processing these tags must recognize that 'DE-DE-U-CO-PHONEBK' and 'de-de-u-co-phonebk' are the same tag, but they should canonicalize it to the lowercase form for storage and comparison. This standardization ensures interoperability across platforms and services that handle localization.
sections.eli5: The rules for 'standard form' mean that 'DE-DE-U-CO' and 'de-de-u-co' mean the same thing, but computers normalize them both to lowercase so they can be compared easily.
